title: Solo dev, no terminal: how I’m built a parry-focused browser beat ’em up with AI (playable, gamepad + mobile) Claude + Codex
author: Agreeable-Gap5500
selftext:
I’ve been building **Empty Fist Taro**, a single-plane side-scrolling beat ’em up with fighting-game controls: two attack buttons, a grab, motion-input specials, and parrying as the core mechanic. It runs in the browser, works with a gamepad, and has touch controls for mobile. It’s still in development (v0.9.081), and I wanted to share how it’s actually being made, because I invested way more time than I expected.

**Who does what.** I’m the designer and "director". Claude writes the code: plain JavaScript on a canvas, no engine or framework. GPT generates the pixel-art sprites from my prompts, and GPT's Codex handles art cleanup in a separate art folder, guided by notes Claude leaves for it. I don’t use a terminal at all. I work through GitHub Desktop, Claude creates the branches, and I build and test locally. The rule that saved the project: Claude has to tell me exactly what it’s going to change and wait for my yes before building anything. 

**Tests and iteration are what make AI code "controlled".** The game runs on a fixed timestep (1/120 s), so behavior is deterministic and testable down to the frame. There are now about 800 automated tests, plus a bot that plays through Level 1 before every release. When Claude changes timing on a move, a test that counts frames will catch it, and Claude has to say whether the test was wrong or the change broke something.

**The background effects, and the usage trap.** The latest update added animated effects over the painted backgrounds: embers and firelight in the burning shrine, waterfalls, drifting leaves and mist in the bamboo forest, lake shimmer and swaying lanterns in the village. They’re drawn on top of the static art rather than redrawing it, and they run on the game clock, so they freeze during hit-stop and parry freezes, which looks better. The first stage burned through a huge amount of my usage, because the AI kept polishing in loops. The fix was a blind critic: a separate cheap model that only sees screenshots, never code, and judges them (I would hope) like a player would. Add a hard cap of two critic rounds, and the next stages came out about as good for potentially a fraction of the cost.

**Video to sprite animation.** Taro’s new idle animation (breathing, a body bob, blinking) started as an AI-generated video clip. A script finds one exact breath cycle by tracking his head height, cuts it into a 12-frame loop, removes the background, locks his feet so they don’t wobble, and adds a blink. Then Codex recolored the sheet for his alternate Gi version. My first loop had a stutter on the way up because it picked frames by similarity instead of following the breath. That’s a good lesson for anyone trying this.

**What AI is still bad at:** character consistency across sprite frames takes a lot of re-rolling and cleanup, and any visual judgment needs a human (or at least a second set of eyes) in the loop. I’ve rejected plenty of “improvements,” like tree sway that made the village roofs wobble. Shifting pixels have their place in low budget effects, not this time.

Play it free in your browser: [HERE](https://melzworld.itch.io/empty-fist-taro). I’d love feedback on the controls and the parry timing. And a question for the sub: **for those using AI for sprites, how are you keeping characters consistent across animation frames?** That’s my biggest remaining bottleneck.

Also, I would also appreciate anyone who wants to be a play tester who enjoys this weird niche of Beat'em Up crossed over with Street Fighter commands mixed in with a little rogue-lite.
